text: Revisiting cyclical framework: industry consolidation unlikely in near term, momentum of earnings cuts accelerating

We revisit our cyclical framework for the China OEM space amid a sharply declining domestic market (volumes -19% YTD), partially offset by a strong acceleration in exports (+70% YTD). Our framework requires three parameters to be hit for industry consolidation to happen: (1) OEMs at cash cost level; (2) management capitulating on profitability & expansion; (3) OEMs' balance sheets turning to net debt.

Industry consolidation unlikely in the near term. As shown in Exhibit 1, as of 1Q26: (1) The majority (10 out of 14) of OEMs are above cash cost level; (2) Management outlooks are mixed on volume/margin/capacity; (3) Only 1 out of 14 OEMs are in a net debt position. Looking ahead, consensus estimates assume more OEMs will turn EBITDA positive in 2027, likely driven by overseas expansion (which offsets domestic decline) and internal organizational restructuring exercises to cut operating expenses, implying no industry consolidation in the near term.

■ Momentum of earnings cuts accelerating. As illustrated in Exhibit 2, aggregate 2026E/2027E EBITDA consensus estimates for China OEMs have undergone four consecutive rounds of cuts over the last year, but the majority are still above cash cost levels. The momentum of cuts has been accelerating, with the last coming in at -4% post 1Q26 results, or a Rmb1.7bn/1.8bn downward revision to the industry total.

We lower our industry volume forecast by 5% in 2026E to reflect the declining domestic retail sales, despite strong export growth. We now model a -9% yoy domestic retail PV volume decline with +30% yoy export growth in 2026E, amounting to largely stable wholesale and production volume vs. 2025. We forecast 2026E NEV penetration at 60%, implying +1% yoy domestic retail NEV volume growth. Among our coverage, we believe BYD (Buy), Leapmotor (Buy) and XPeng (Buy) are better positioned for both domestic volume growth acceleration as well as higher overseas exposure, with accelerating new export model pipelines and sales network expansion.

text: Bottom line: Based on our three watch points below, the majority of the OEMs are still above cash cost with overall industry cash profit increasing in 2025/1Q26. On the other hand, the industry’s cash position declined in 2025/1Q26 due to shortening payable cycles under government guidelines. Management teams expect strong overseas demand to mitigate domestic weakness, with mixed views on margin going into the next few quarters. At the same time, more companies are focusing on expanding overseas production. Overall we believe that 1) industry consolidation is yet to come amid a higher industry cash profit level, 2) stabilizing margins, supported by overseas sales and improved product mix, will mitigate domestic competition and cost pressure, and 3) increasing demand for equity issuance could stabilize the industry’s cash position.

1. OEMs at cash cost level: 11 out of 14 OEMs had positive EBITDA in 2025, vs. 10 in 2024. Auto OEM industry EBITDA continues to grow with ongoing cost-cutting measures (today's lowest priced NEV is c.US\$4k) and a profit contribution from strong export growth.

2. Management capitulating on profitability & expansion: Although domestic demand is weaker than initial outlooks at the beginning of this year for most OEMs, strong export volume has supported overall volume growth. Management teams have mixed views on margin with some OEMs expecting lower sequential margins due to ongoing cost pressures, and others anticipating improving margins driven by higher volume and product mix. Also, we note that more OEMs are considering overseas capacity expansion.

3. Calculating potential tipping point: Profitable OEMs on average have room to cut prices by 14% to maintain cash cost break-even, and certain loss-making OEMs could fall into a net debt position in 2028 and beyond without further funding, in our view.

We refresh our inflection point framework for the China autos space post 1Q26 results, following our last edition - China Automobiles: Revisiting inflection framework: Capex expansion & competition amid slowing growth into 2026 (published in Jan 2026).

We believe the OEM industry inflection point will materialize when the majority of companies are at or near cash cost level, i.e. the EBITDA break-even point. This would imply that cash flows for the majority of the industry have deteriorated to the point at which companies are no longer able to add any new capacity and/or have begun to take capacity off-line.

As of 2025/1Q26, 11/9 out of 14 OEMs had positive EBITDA, compared to 10/10 in 2024/1Q25. Meanwhile, OEM aggregate industry EBITDA increased by 6%/11% yoy in 2025/1Q26 (vs. 34%/15% yoy in 2024/1Q25). On the other hand, industry net cash declined by Rmb65bn in 1Q26 vs. 1Q25, mainly due to shortening payable days (especially for BYD). Accordingly, we expect the industry inflection point to be dragged out for a longer period due to strong cash profit generation despite lower net cash positions.

text: On the other hand, we saw margin stabilization among suppliers in 1Q26, mainly on the contribution from battery systems, with gross margin/EBITDA margin/EBIT margin +1.0pp/-0.3pp/-0.1pp yoy in 1Q26. By segment, there was a divergence in profitability among suppliers in 1Q26, with stronger revenue growth/higher margins for battery systems and pressured revenues/margin deterioration for other suppliers. For battery systems, revenue growth was strong (+40% yoy, vs. 16.2% yoy for all suppliers excluding outliers) and EBIT margins improved (+1.9pp yoy, vs. -0.4pp yoy for all suppliers excluding outliers), mainly driven by strong ESS demand and price increases amid raw material cost inflation. Meanwhile, other suppliers' revenue came under pressure given weak demand in 1Q26 and OEMs tried to optimize costs across other supply chains to mitigate lithium price increases. In terms of balance sheet, we continued to see pressure – OEMs' net cash decreased by Rmb65bn yoy and there was a +7pp increase in the total debt-to-equity ratio in 1Q26, while suppliers (excluding outliers) saw a Rmb29bn yoy increase in net debt and +4pp yoy increase in the total debt-to-equity ratio. The total liability-to-asset ratio remained relatively stable for both OEMs and suppliers as a whole.

text: We believe the industry will start to consolidate when management teams become pessimistic about both the industry and their own company's outlook, which is when we would expect them to start cutting back on capex and opex. Thereafter, industry supply-demand could begin to rebalance with a potential operating leverage turn-around.

Consensus - We note that management teams tend to agree on domestic demand being weak and the export outlook being strong, leading to an industry consensus to cut domestic ICE capacity while seeing more discussions to expand overseas (especially in Europe). Debates - Management teams are different on the timeline for cost pressures to be fully reflected and profit to bottom out, and thus there are mixed views on volume/margin depending on companies' product cycles and overseas exposure.

\- Mixed views on volume guidance: Based on management teams' commentary on the overall industry, they share similar views on weak domestic demand mitigated by a stronger-than-expected export outlook, leading to a mixed volume outlook depending on their domestic model cycles and overseas exposure.

☐ Weaker domestic demand: Management teams are on the same page in anticipating a high-single-digit to low-teens decline in domestic demand this year (vs. -5% to +1% yoy growth per most management teams during our 2026 mgmt outlook call series at the beginning of 2026).

☐ Stronger export outlook: On the other hand, exports continue to beat management expectations, driven especially by high oil prices post the Middle East crisis. Multiple OEMs have raised their export guidance.

☐ Competition shifts from price to technology: Within the mass market, BYD aims to improve market share, driven mainly by new technology rather than price competition. Management teams also highlighted more crowded competition within the premium segment (e.g. large 6-seater SUVs). Seres believes Chinese brands will continue to take share from foreign premium brands, and Li Auto/Nio expect potential consolidation on the back of technology (e.g. embodied AI) and increasing brand awareness. Meanwhile, XPeng sees its premiumization as well on track, evidenced by strong orders for GX models.
☐ Different timelines on when cost pressures are reflected...: Some OEMs believe cost pressure was already reflected in earnings in 1Q26, while others see continued pressure into 2Q26/3Q26.

☐ ...resulting in diverging margin trajectories: As a result, some OEMs expect lower sequential margins from ongoing cost pressures, while others look for margin improvement driven by higher volume and product mix.

Consensus view on lowering domestic ICE capacity and expanding overseas: Management teams generally plan to continue reducing ICE capacity domestically, while having more discussions about expanding overseas production capacity, especially in Europe (e.g. BYD, SAIC, Chery, Great Wall, XPeng).

text: We carry out an analysis to assess the potential tipping point for different OEMs as to when they could reach EBITDA break-even point and the timing of net cash exhaustion.

For the group of OEMs with positive EBITDA in 1Q26, our analysis suggests that they may have capacity for further 5%-24% price cuts before getting to cash cost (vs. 4%-18% in 1Q25); for the OEMs with EBITDA losses but with continued net cash on hand in 1Q26, our analysis suggests that all would fall into a net debt position from 2028 or beyond (except for GAC, which is already in net debt), vs. tipping points in Aug 2025 for Nio, 2026 for Leapmotor and XPeng, and post-2027 for GAC based on our analysis as of 1Q25.
For OEMs with positive EBITDA, we try to answer the question: At what price would these OEMs get to EBITDA of zero?

We note that 9 OEMs had positive EBITDA as of 1Q26 (vs. 12/10 in 4Q25/1Q25), and we calculate the unit EBITDA for these companies in Exhibit 14. We assume that unit EBITDA value is equivalent to the magnitude of price cuts it takes to get to an EBITDA of zero. For these 9 OEMs, their 1Q26 blended ASP ex-VAT (calculated by dividing vehicle revenue by vehicle sales volume) ranges from Rmb79k to Rmb347k (vs. Rmb77k to Rmb265k for 9 OEMs with positive EBITDA in 1Q25).
Conclusion: Our calculation implies a price cut range of 5%-24% for these companies (vs. 4%-18% in 1Q25) (Exhibit 15).

text: For OEMs with negative EBITDA but in a net cash position, we try to answer the question: How many months will it take to eliminate the net cash position at the current rate of loss?

We note 3 OEMs are loss-making on an EBITDA level, but still had net cash on their balance sheets as of 1Q26 (GAC has negative EBITDA and was already in a net debt position). We calculate the unit EBITDA loss for these companies and assume a similar rate of unit EBITDA loss going forward, based on which we estimate how many months it would take to exhaust the net cash on hand. Our monthly sales assumptions are either based on our published models for covered companies, or on the monthly average of annual consensus volume estimates for Not Covered names.
Conclusion: Our analysis suggests that all would move into a net debt position no earlier than 2028 or beyond, with XPeng shifting from net cash to net debt in Mar 2028 due to cost pressures in 1Q26 (pulled in by 9+ months vs. estimates using 2025 unit EBITDA/2025 net cash), and Li Auto/Leapmotor doing so only after 2028 (Exhibit 16).

text: Revising our industry model with lower domestic and higher export volume

We lower our PV retail volume forecasts for the domestic market by 3%-8% over 2020E-2030E, mainly reflecting weaker-than-expected domestic demand in 5M26 driven by 1) a lower trade-in subsidy in 2026 compared to 2025, 2) a higher NEV purchase tax starting in 2026, and 3) the declining effectiveness of subsidies with demand already being pulled forward in 2024 and 2025.

On the other hand, we raise our China passenger vehicle export volume forecast by 6%-11% over 2026E-2030E, expecting 7.8mn units in 2026E rising to 10mn in 2030E (accounting for 17% of market share ex-China/US). Among this, we expect NEV penetration to increase from 49% to 70%, translating to a 26% CAGR over the next five years, underpinned by accelerating NEV penetration from both increased model supply with both improved features and cost competitiveness vs. ICE.
Net-net, we revise our forecast for China passenger vehicle production/wholesale volume by -5% to +1% over 2026E-2030E, primarily due to weak domestic demand offset by strong export momentum.

text: Buy BYD, Leapmotor and XPeng on domestic recovery and overseas upside potential

Among our coverage companies, we believe BYD (Buy), Leapmotor (Buy) and XPeng (Buy) are better positioned to benefit from a sequential acceleration in domestic sales, as well accelerating overseas momentum i.e. new export model pipelines and sales network expansion, given their greater overseas exposure.
BYD (002594.SZ, 1211.HK; Buy) - Domestic recovery set in motion with overseas acceleration

Domestic recovery set in motion: Domestically, we believe BYD's retail sales recovery has been set in motion, as the company launches new models with technology innovation (e.g. 2nd generation blade battery + flash charging ecosystem) to enhance its competitive strengths in China (see our report), as well as most affordable urban NOA model (Rmb78.8k) and 1-year comprehensive safety liability guarantee for its urban NOA (see our report).

For flash-charging capabilities, we believe BYD is now building a comprehensive flash-charging ecosystem from battery, charging, and storage to models, to effectively strengthen its competitive moat, making it difficult for peers to catch up, at least in the short term. For intelligent development, BYD announced that God's Eye B (featuring urban NOA) is now available for all models (package priced at Rmb12k), which effectively makes the entry model price Rmb78.8k, the most affordable in the China market at present; BYD also unveiled its first in-house 4-nm smart driving chip Xuanji A3, which could potentially lower component cost and improve profit levels.

As evidenced by recent strong order intake (e.g. 100k pre-sales orders for Da Tang; 30k orders for Yuan Plus in the first week of facelift launch) and retail numbers (182k units of domestic sales in Apr, improving NEV market share to $21.4\%$ in April from $15.8\%$ in Jan), we believe BYD's domestic sales momentum should continue, demonstrating that a recovery has been set in motion, at least in the following months.

text: Overseas market to become a major growth driver: We expect the overseas market to become a key growth driver over the next decade for the company and model BYD's overseas (ex-US) sales volume at 1.7mn-3.5mn in 2026E-2035E. We forecast a $30\%$ earnings CAGR over 2026E-2028E, with overseas profit contribution to increase from $21\%$ in 2024 to $81\%$ by 2028E, accounting for more than half of our valuation. Key

1. NEV penetration ramp into mass-adoption phase supported by increasing model supply: Currently we see NEV penetration in key overseas markets as around 4 years behind China (i.e. 4Q21 level) on average at $22\%$ . This is around the starting point of mass-adoption that we observed in China and we expect the overseas markets to follow China's $>10\%$ penetration increase trajectory (i.e. 2022-2024) in the upcoming years. Such mass-adoption should also be supported by increasing new model supply offering new features and cost competitiveness vs. ICE.

2. BYD product competitiveness driving market share gain: Based on our product comp analysis, BYD's models are highly competitive in key aspects including price, range, and size. Going forward, with a comprehensive portfolio of models readily developed in the domestic market, ongoing R&D investment, and expansion of sales network, we believe BYD is well positioned to take top volume market share among global NEV companies.

text: Leapmotor (9863.HK; Buy) - Domestic growth acceleration with overseas volume upside
See our initiation report: Domestic growth acceleration with overseas volume upside, valuation discount unwarranted; Initiate at Buy

We expect Leapmotor, a leading pure NEV player with 5.1% market share in China (5M26) per CPCA, to execute a series of competitive new model launches with smooth production ramp-up, that should drive continued growth acceleration in the domestic market over the next three quarters (Exhibit 26); at the same time, we see 60% upside to the company's 2026 overseas target sales volume of 125k units (implying +108% yoy) at the mid-point (i.e. GSe 200k units), supported by strong overseas retail sales which were up +554% yoy during 1Q26 (Exhibit 28). Overall, we forecast Leapmotor to deliver one of the fastest revenue/earnings CAGRs (2025-27E) at 48%/143% among our China Mobility Tech coverage, yet the stock is currently trading at a c.60% discount to peers on both P/E and P/S (Exhibit 29). We are Buy rated on Leapmotor, with a 12-m DCF-based TP of HK\$50. Catalysts include new model launches, monthly delivery ramp-up and export acceleration to fulfill retail-end demand. On the other hand, risks of worsening domestic market demand, cost inflation, and uncertainty overseas could exert pressure on volume/margins and cash flow.

Where we are different from consensus: Our 2026E-28E net income estimates are $7\% - 12\%$ above the Visible Alpha consensus, mainly driven by $3\% - 7\%$ higher volume estimates. Our higher volume assumptions mainly come from overseas markets, where Leapmotor models rank Top3 based on our product comparison framework, and we expect strong retail-end demand to drive further acceleration in the company's monthly export growth.

Financials & Risks: We forecast a 36% revenue CAGR (2025-28E), mainly driven by 37% vehicle volume growth from 583k to 1,496k, while we expect continued pricing pressure in China's EV market to result in further ASP reduction. We forecast a 38% gross profit CAGR (2025-28E) with gross margin improving from 14.5% to 14.9% mainly driven by improving economies of scale despite increasing cost pressure. The company turned free cash flow positive in 2024 and net profit break-even in 2025 with Rmb11.5bn net cash at end-2025, and we expect ongoing positive FCF generation with net margin improving to 5.1% in 2028E. Key risks: Industry demand, cost inflation, overseas uncertainty.

In addition to NEVs, XPeng is also making solid progress in transforming itself into a physical AI company. 2026 will be a year of volume production for a number of emerging businesses in our view: (1) autonomous driving based on VLA 2.0 model to develop generalization capability, targeting to release VLA 2.0 Version 2 in 3Q26, which operates without HD maps and which could substantially elevate model performance limits, (2) robotaxi trial operation on GX's L4 full redundancy hardware and software to validate the Robotaxi business model in China, (3) humanoid robots to start volume production in 2026, expecting revenues from humanoid robot hardware and AI models to emerge as a key driver for revenue size of billions of Rmb starting in 2027 per the company.

The GS Factor Profile provides investment context for a stock by comparing key attributes to the market (i.e. our universe of rated stocks) and its sector peers. The four key attributes depicted are: Growth, Financial Returns, Multiple (e.g. valuation) and Integrated (a composite of Growth, Financial Returns and Multiple). Growth, Financial Returns and Multiple are calculated by using normalized ranks for specific metrics for each stock. The normalized ranks for the metrics are then averaged and converted into percentiles for the relevant attribute. The precise calculation of each metric may vary depending on the fiscal year, industry and region, but the standard approach is as follows:

Growth is based on a stock's forward-looking sales growth, EBITDA growth and EPS growth (for financial stocks, only EPS and sales growth), with a higher percentile indicating a higher growth company. Financial Returns is based on a stock's forward-looking ROE, ROCE and CROCI (for financial stocks, only ROE), with a higher percentile indicating a company with higher financial returns. Multiple is based on a stock's forward-looking P/E, P/B, price/dividend (P/D), EV/EBITDA, EV/FCF and EV/Debt Adjusted Cash Flow (DACF) (for financial stocks, only P/E, P/B and P/D), with a higher percentile indicating a stock trading at a higher multiple. The Integrated percentile is calculated as the average of the Growth percentile, Financial Returns percentile and (100% - Multiple percentile).

Financial Returns and Multiple use the GS analyst forecasts at the fiscal year-end at least three quarters in the future. Growth uses inputs for the fiscal year at least seven quarters in the future compared with the year at least three quarters in the future (on a per-share basis for all metrics).
For a more detailed description of how we calculate the GS Factor Profile, please contact your GS representative.

Across our global coverage, we examine stocks using an M&A framework, considering both qualitative factors and quantitative factors (which may vary across sectors and regions) to incorporate the potential that certain companies could be acquired. We then assign a M&A rank as a means of scoring companies under our rated coverage from 1 to 3, with 1 representing high (30%-50%) probability of the company becoming an acquisition target, 2 representing medium (15%-30%) probability and 3 representing low (0%-15%) probability. For companies ranked 1 or 2, in line with our standard departmental guidelines we incorporate an M&A component into our target price. M&A rank of 3 is considered immaterial and therefore does not factor into our price target, and may or may not be discussed in research.
